source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, indeed, an Apostle, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, afterwards changing the sword to a stylus, and converting the sword to a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! When rejoicing about the Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to the Romans: Not only, indeed, but also rejoicing in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly probation, probation indeed hope, hope indeed does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, co-heirs truly of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider the passions of this time not to be worthy of the glory which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what has been written: For Your sake we are killed all day, we have been considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own passions, he has predetermined that we must suffer: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. If these seem more like hardships than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding words: We are troubled in all things, but not constrained; and we are in need, but not in extreme need; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; we are cast down, but not destroyed: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but our inner man is being renewed day by day; namely the soul by the hope of promises. For what is present, temporal and light, our pressure, through surpassing, surpasses into eternal weight of glory, not looking at what is seen, but at what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking about hardships; what is not seen is eternal, promising about rewards. To the Thessalonians, indeed, writing about his chains, he has affirmed that those are blessed to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having, he says, the same struggle which you saw in me and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in the same way. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, by which he acquires solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his own prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion. It is sufficient that he also spoke above: A faithful word: if we have died with Christ, and live with Him; if we suffer, and reign with Him; if we deny, and He denies us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. Therefore, do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me being bound by Him; because He has foretold: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, and love, and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer on account of innocence. But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than to those who suffer martyrdoms? Where he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

bible_refs.note: Who will separate us from the love of Christ?
I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.

pass_b_english: Paul the Apostle—once a persecutor who spilled the Church's first blood—swapped sword for stylus, hammered his blade into a plowshare. The ravening wolf of Benjamin turned around and brought provisions, just as Jacob said. And this is how he commends martyrdoms, now desirable even to himself! Rejoicing over the Thessalonians, he says: we boast about you in God's churches because of your endurance and faith amid every persecution and pressure you bear—proof of God's just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you also suffer (2 Thess 1:4-5). He writes the same to the Romans: not only that, but we exult in pressures, knowing that pressure produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom 5:3-5). And again: if we are children, then heirs—heirs of God, co-heirs with Christ—provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him (Rom 8:17). I consider the sufferings of this present time not worth comparing to the glory that will be revealed in us (Rom 8:18). And so he adds: who will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword—as it is written: "For your sake we are killed all day long; we were accounted as sheep for slaughter." Yet in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through the one who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death nor life nor power nor height nor depth nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:35-39).

To the Corinthians he catalogs his own sufferings, declaring that suffering is non-negotiable: in labors more abundantly, in imprisonments more excessively, in near-deaths often. Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; and the rest (2 Cor 11:23-25). If these look more like hardships than martyrdoms, he insists again: therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake (2 Cor 12:10). Earlier he wrote: we are afflicted in every way but not crushed; perplexed but not driven to despair; persecuted but not forsaken; struck down but not destroyed—always carrying in the body the death of Jesus (2 Cor 4:8-10). Even if, he says, our outer self is wasting away—our flesh, by the force of persecutions—our inner self is being renewed day by day, our soul by the hope of promises (2 Cor 4:16). For this slight momentary affliction prepares for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, because we look not at what is seen but at what is unseen. What is seen is temporary—he speaks of hardships; what is unseen is eternal—he promises rewards (2 Cor 4:17-18).

Writing to the Thessalonians about his chains, he pronounces blessed those to whom it has been granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him: having the same conflict you saw in me and now hear about (Phil 1:29-30). Even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice of your faith, I rejoice and share my joy with you all; likewise you also rejoice and share your joy with me (Phil 2:17-18). You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, which gains its solemnity from mutual joy. So he draws near to his own desire: writing to Timothy, exulting in his prospect? "For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown, which the Lord will render to me on that day—the crown of suffering" (2 Tim 4:6-8). It is enough that he also said above: "The saying is trustworthy: if we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful—he cannot deny himself" (2 Tim 2:11-13). So do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; for he foretold: "God gave us not a spirit of fear but of power and love and self-control" (2 Tim 1:7-8). We suffer with power, from love for God, and with a sound mind, because we suffer for innocence's sake. But where he commands endurance—to whom does he point it more than to those who face martyrdom? Where he tears people away from idolatry—what does he tear them toward more than martyrdom?

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that includes necessary scripture citations (e.g., Rom 8:35-39, 2 Tim 4:6-8) which were not present in the Latin but are required for the English reader to identify the quoted passages. All clauses, including the complex descriptions of Paul's transformation and the enumeration of his sufferings, are preserved.

Tertullian's Latin text, Pass A, and Pass B are consistent with the supplied source. The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, and all scriptural citations match the quoted content. The title 'Martyrdom' appropriately captures the central theme of the passage.
